name: accept4
synopsis: int accept(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *_Nullable restrict addr, socklen_t *_Nullable restrict addrlen);
int accept4(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *_Nullable restrict addr, socklen_t *_Nullable restrict addrlen, int flags);
description: The accept4() system call is used with connection-based socket types to extract the first pending connection request for a listening socket and create a new connected socket. It returns a new file descriptor and allows additional flags to modify the new socket's behavior, such as setting it to non-blocking or close-on-exec.

parameters.name: sockfd
parameters.description: The file descriptor of the listening socket.

parameters.name: addr
parameters.description: Pointer to a sockaddr structure to receive the address of the connecting peer.

parameters.name: addrlen
parameters.description: Pointer to the size of the addr structure, which is a value-result argument.

parameters.name: flags
parameters.description: Flags to modify the new socket's behavior, such as SOCK_NONBLOCK or SOCK_CLOEXEC.

return_value.success: Returns a nonnegative integer file descriptor for the accepted socket.
return_value.failure: Returns -1 on error, and errno is set to indicate the error.

errors.description: The socket is marked nonblocking and no connections are present.
sockfd is not an open file descriptor.
The addr argument is not in a writable part of the user address space.
The system call was interrupted by a signal.
Socket is not listening, addrlen is invalid, or flags is invalid for accept4().
The per-process limit on open file descriptors has been reached.
The system-wide limit on open files has been reached.
sockfd does not refer to a socket.
The socket is not of type SOCK_STREAM.

bugs: On Linux, the new socket does not inherit file status flags like O_NONBLOCK from the listening socket, differing from BSD behavior; portable programs should explicitly set flags.
